options.text: The cost of the single most expensive operation
The average cost per operation over a worst-case sequence of operations
The best-case cost of one operation
The memory used across all operations

questions.explanation: Amortized analysis averages cost over a sequence so occasional expensive operations are paid for by many cheap ones. It is a worst-case guarantee on the sequence, not a probabilistic average.

questions.prompt: Why is appending to a dynamic array O(1) amortized despite occasional O(n) resizes?

options.text: The array is always full
Resizes never actually copy elements
Doubling capacity makes resizes geometrically rare, so their cost spreads to O(1) per append
Appends are done in parallel

questions.explanation: Because capacity doubles, the total copying work over n appends is at most 2n, so each append averages O(1). Growing by a constant instead would make appends O(n) amortized.

questions.prompt: The accounting (banker's) method of amortized analysis works by:

options.text: Ignoring the expensive operations
Assuming all operations cost the same
Measuring the exact time of each operation
Charging cheap operations extra to build credit that pays for later expensive ones

questions.explanation: Overcharging inexpensive operations stores credit that covers the rare costly ones, keeping the balance non-negative. The potential method is a related technique using a potential function.

questions.prompt: Randomized quicksort achieves expected O(n log n) time because random pivots:

options.text: Guarantee a perfectly balanced split every time
Make consistently unbalanced partitions extremely unlikely regardless of input order
Sort the array before partitioning
Eliminate all comparisons

questions.explanation: Choosing the pivot at random decouples performance from the input arrangement, so no particular input triggers the O(n^2) worst case. The expectation over random choices is O(n log n).

questions.prompt: A Las Vegas randomized algorithm is one that:

options.text: May return a wrong answer with small probability
Always runs in the same time
Always returns a correct answer, with running time that varies randomly
Never uses randomness

questions.explanation: Las Vegas algorithms guarantee correctness but their runtime is a random variable — randomized quicksort is an example. Monte Carlo algorithms trade the opposite way: fixed time, small error probability.

questions.prompt: A Monte Carlo randomized algorithm is one that:

options.text: Uses no random choices
Is always correct but may run slowly
Never terminates
Runs in bounded time but may be wrong with small probability

questions.explanation: Monte Carlo methods fix the running time and accept a small chance of error, which repeated runs can drive down. The Miller-Rabin primality test is a well-known example.

questions.prompt: A skip list uses randomization to achieve expected O(log n) search by:

options.text: Balancing via rotations like an AVL tree
Promoting elements to higher express lanes with a random coin flip
Sorting the list on every insertion
Hashing each element

questions.explanation: Random level assignment creates a hierarchy of shortcut lists that skip over many elements, giving balanced-tree-like performance in expectation without explicit rebalancing. It is a simpler alternative to a balanced BST.

questions.prompt: In the potential method of amortized analysis, the amortized cost of an operation is:

options.text: The maximum over all operations
Always equal to its actual cost
Its actual cost plus the change in a potential function
Its actual cost divided by the number of operations

questions.explanation: Defining a potential that stores prepaid work, the amortized cost is the real cost plus the potential's change, and summing telescopes to bound the total. It generalises the accounting method.

questions.prompt: A Bloom filter is a randomized structure that answers set membership with:

options.text: False negatives but no false positives
No errors at all
Exact membership like a hash set
No false negatives but a tunable rate of false positives, using little space

questions.explanation: Multiple hash functions set bits in a compact array; a query is definitely-absent or probably-present, so it never misses a real member but can falsely include one. This trades a small error rate for large space savings.

questions.prompt: Why can the amortized cost of an operation be lower than its worst-case single-operation cost?

options.text: Amortized cost ignores expensive operations
Expensive operations occur rarely and their cost is spread over many cheap ones in the sequence
Operations run concurrently
The worst case never actually happens

questions.explanation: Amortized analysis accounts for the whole sequence, so a costly resize or rebuild that happens once every n operations contributes only O(1) per operation on average. It still counts every operation, unlike average-case analysis over random inputs.
